intro: A spoon of sugar vanishes into tea. A puddle dries up and leaves nothing behind. A balloon that looks empty pushes back when you squeeze it. A friend across a noisy gym reads a message you sent with nothing but a blinking flashlight. Each of these is a puzzle about things you cannot see.

This unit gives you tools to solve those puzzles. The first tool is a balance. With it you will prove that sugar, air and melted ice are still there, even when your eyes say otherwise. The second tool is a picture in your mind: matter as tiny particles, always moving, never lost.

Then you will follow the patterns that move through matter: waves in a rope, sound in the air, light bouncing off a mirror or bending in water. By the end, you will be able to explain why a straw looks broken in a glass, how a code turns blinks into words, and why a text message crosses the world without a single wrong letter.
bigQuestion: How can we know what matter is made of and what waves carry, when both are too small or too fast to see?

timeline.t: Democritus argues that everything is made of tiny pieces moving in empty space
Ibn al-Haytham's Book of Optics: we see because light enters the eye
Isaac Newton reports that a prism splits white sunlight into colors
Antoine Lavoisier shows with careful weighing that mass is conserved in every change
John Dalton explains chemical changes as rearrangements of atoms
Robert Brown sees pollen grains jiggle in water, a clue to unseen moving particles
Samuel Morse sends the first public telegraph message in dots and dashes
Alexander Graham Bell's telephone turns a voice into an electric signal
Albert Einstein explains the jiggling pollen as kicks from invisible water particles
The scanning tunneling microscope lets scientists make pictures of single atoms

words.d: anything that has mass and takes up space
the amount of stuff in an object, measured with a balance
one of the tiny pieces that all matter is made of
the rule that the total amount of matter stays the same through a change
to break into particles so small they spread through a liquid and cannot be seen
a feature of a material that you can observe or measure
a change that makes new substances with new properties
a repeating pattern of motion that carries energy through a material
the height of a wave; a measure of its energy
the distance from one crest of a wave to the next
the bending of light when it passes from one material into another
a code that uses only two signals, on and off, written as 1 and 0

test.why: Air has mass and takes up space. Light, shadows and songs do not have mass.

test.q: Why do scientists use a particle model?
choices: Models are easier to draw than real things
Particles are real but far too small to see
Models replace the need for experiments
test.why: A model stands in for something real we cannot see directly. Particles are real but tiny.

test.q: A sealed bag of ice is weighed, melts, and is weighed again. The mass:
test.why: Melting changes solid to liquid but no particles leave the sealed bag.

test.q: A student stirs salt into water until it vanishes. The salt:
choices: Is still there, spread out as tiny particles
test.why: The salt dissolved. Its particles are too small to see, but the mass and the taste prove they are there.

test.q: Baking soda and vinegar fizz in an open cup and the mass drops. The best explanation is:
choices: A gas escaped into the air
test.why: The bubbles are a gas. When they pop and float away, they take their mass with them.

test.q: Which is a property you could use to identify a material?
test.why: Magnetism is a feature of the material itself that you can test. Price and age are not properties of the material.

test.q: Which change makes a new substance?
test.why: The fizz is carbon dioxide, a new substance with new properties. The other changes can be undone.

test.q: A wave passes a floating leaf. The leaf:
choices: Bobs up and down and stays near its spot
test.why: Waves move the water up and down. The energy travels on, but the water and the leaf stay close.

test.q: A wave with a bigger amplitude:
test.why: Amplitude is the height of a wave, and a taller wave carries more energy.

test.q: You hold a paper near a loud speaker and it flutters. This shows that:
choices: Sound waves carry energy that can move objects
Light from the speaker pushes the paper
test.why: Sound is a wave of pushes in the air. Its energy reached the paper and moved it.

test.q: In a completely dark room you cannot see a chair because:
choices: No light reflects off the chair into your eyes
test.why: Seeing needs light bouncing off an object into your eyes. With no light, nothing reaches them.

test.q: A straw in a glass of water looks broken because:
choices: Light bends as it passes from water into air
The water pushes the straw sideways
test.why: Refraction bends the light from the underwater part, so your eye sees it in the wrong place.

test.q: In Morse code, the letter O is:
test.why: O is three long signals, or dashes. S is three dots.

test.q: With 4 bits, how many different patterns can you make?
test.why: Each added bit doubles the count: 2, 4, 8, 16.

test.q: Why can a digital message cross an ocean without errors?
choices: Bits are sent as light only
Receivers only decide on or off and send fresh copies
test.why: Even a weak flash is clearly on, not off. A receiver copies the bits cleanly and sends them on.

write.prompt: Make a claim: when sugar disappears into water, is the sugar still there? Support it with evidence from the balance test and from what happens when the water dries. Then explain how the particle model makes sense of that evidence.
tips: Claim: say clearly whether the sugar is still there and in what form.
Evidence: use the mass before and after stirring, and the crystals left after drying.
Reasoning: explain how particles too small to see can still have mass and be tasted.
The other side: what would someone who thinks the sugar is gone expect the balance to show?
Compare: how is this different from baking soda fizzing in vinegar?
